question: What is the simplest way to describe what a drug does in the body?

options.A: Any synthetic material used strictly for laboratory testing
options.B: A compound that creates entirely new cellular functions in organs
options.C: Any chemical substance that alters biological function in a living body
options.D: A natural substance derived exclusively from plants for nourishment

explanation: Spot on! Drugs work by modifying what your body is already doing—they don't magically invent brand-new functions. You've got this! [learn more](GNS125_U1_T3#GNS125_U1_T3_h1)

question: How do medications interact with our cells?

options.A: By permanently replacing vital organs with chemical substitutes
options.B: By modifying or blocking already existing cellular activities
options.C: By changing the basic genetic code of the target organ
options.D: By destroying diseased cells and generating brand new tissues

explanation: Great job! Think of drugs as little keys that speed up, slow down, or block processes your body already knows how to do. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T3#GNS125_U1_T3_h1)

question: Morphine and digitalis are famous examples of drugs gotten from which natural source?
explanation: You got it! Many powerful medicines we use today started out as active chemical extracts from plants. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T3#GNS125_U1_T3_h2)

question: Why do modern pharmaceutical companies love making synthetic drugs in labs instead of relying only on natural plants?

options.A: Synthetic drugs offer better purity, consistency, and mass production
options.B: Natural plant sources have completely disappeared from the earth
options.C: Synthetic drugs never cause any form of allergic reaction in humans
options.D: Laboratory chemicals are always much cheaper to discover and test

explanation: Exactly! Making drugs in a lab lets companies control the exact dosage and produce enough for everyone without waiting for plant harvest seasons. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T3#GNS125_U1_T3_h2)

question: What do we call the special brand name given and copyrighted by the company that makes a drug?
explanation: Spot on! The trade name (or brand name) belongs exclusively to the company that manufactures that particular version of the drug. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T3#GNS125_U1_T3_h3)

question: As a nurse, why is it safest to use a drug's generic name during handovers and charting?

options.A: It is always the shortest name listed in the hospital drug dictionary
options.B: It proves that the drug was manufactured using natural plant sources
options.C: It remains universal and prevents medication errors caused by look-alike trade names
options.D: It guarantees that the medication was produced inside the country

explanation: Brilliant! Generic names never change no matter who makes the pill, which keeps our patients safe from confusing brand names. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T3#GNS125_U1_T3_h3)

question: Why do we bother grouping drugs into different classes?

options.A: To eliminate the need for nurses to check patient vital signs
options.B: To dictate the exact financial cost of each medication in the pharmacy
options.C: To ensure that every drug has exactly one trade name worldwide
options.D: To group medications with similar properties and manage vast pharmaceutical knowledge

explanation: You're right on track! There are thousands of drugs out there, and classification helps us make sense of them by grouping similar ones together. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T3#GNS125_U1_T3_h4)

question: If a patient is given a new drug classed as an antihypertensive, what main effect should you expect?
explanation: Well done! 'Anti' means against, and 'hypertensive' refers to high blood pressure—so antihypertensives bring high blood pressure down. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T3#GNS125_U1_T3_h4)

question: What term describes the study of what the body does to a drug (absorption, distribution, metabolism, and excretion)?
explanation: Nailed it! Pharmacokinetics tracks the journey of the drug through the body across those four famous ADME stages. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T3#GNS125_U1_T3_h5)

question: How is pharmacodynamics different from pharmacokinetics?

options.A: Pharmacodynamics measures drug absorption speed, whereas pharmacokinetics measures patient pulse rates
options.B: Pharmacodynamics only applies to herbal remedies, whereas pharmacokinetics applies to synthetic drugs
options.C: Pharmacodynamics studies how liver enzymes break down pills, whereas pharmacokinetics studies tablet manufacturing
options.D: Pharmacodynamics focuses on drug action and cellular effects, whereas pharmacokinetics focuses on body processing like excretion

explanation: Awesome! Remember: Pharmacokinetics is what the *body* does to the drug, while pharmacodynamics is what the *drug* does to the body. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T3#GNS125_U1_T3_h5)

question: Which agency is responsible for regulating food and drugs here in Nigeria?
explanation: Correct! NAFDAC (National Agency for Food and Drug Administration and Control) keeps our drug supply safe across Nigeria. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T3#GNS125_U1_T3_h6)

question: Why must Nigerian nurses always check the NAFDAC number on drug packaging?

options.A: To calculate the precise half-life of the drug in the patient's bloodstream
options.B: To find out which pharmaceutical company holds the international trade patent
options.C: To confirm the product is legally approved and guard against fake or substandard drugs
options.D: To determine the exact chemical formula of the active ingredient

explanation: Spot on! Checking for that NAFDAC number is a crucial shield against fake or unsafe medications in clinical practice. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T3#GNS125_U1_T3_h6)

question: When are the three safety checks supposed to be done on a medication container?

options.A: When retrieving, preparing, and administering the drug
options.B: At the end of the shift during documentation handover
options.C: Whenever the patient complains of a new side effect
options.D: Only when ordering the medication from the hospital pharmacy

explanation: You got it! Checking the label three times—when you pick it up, when you prep it, and right before giving it—keeps your patient safe. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T3#GNS125_U1_T3_h7)

question: You are about to give an oral med, but you notice the patient's ID band doesn't match the chart. What should you do FIRST?

options.A: Leave the medication at the bedside table for the patient to take later
options.B: Withhold the medication and verify patient identity using the chart and verbal inquiry
options.C: Ask another student nurse to give the medication instead
options.D: Administer the medication anyway since you know the patient's face

explanation: Safety first! Never guess or skip ID checks. Always pause, withhold the drug, and sort out the correct identity before proceeding. [learn more](GNS125_U1_T3#GNS125_U1_T3_h7)
